notes: Catalogue snapshot, not a claim of completeness for undiscovered or unlisted objects. The JPL discovery page retains a 2023-05-23 footer but includes 2026 MPEC references.

Uranus Puck has two fits in the mean-elements table: its newer URA184 solution (2025 epoch) is orbit, while its older URA182 solution is stored in alternateOrbits. Saturn S/2009 S 1 appears in the discovery table only.

The discovery source lists 460 satellites of other worlds; the Earth Moon is present in the mean elements and physical tables. Pluto and its five moons are in both catalogues. The individual records were joined by Pluto and approved name.
Satellite names for JPL codes 519 and 558 follow the discovery table: Megaclite (Jupiter XIX) and Philophrosyne (Jupiter LVIII). The alternate spellings in the mean elements table remain searchable.

Orbital distances are in km, periods in days, angles in degrees, epoch and periapsisJD in TDB Julian days. Source hours for small-body orbital periods were divided by 24. Published punctuation and the approximate marker are retained where present.

Mean elements are averaged approximations, unsuitable for precise ephemerides. The ecliptic and equatorial mean planes are centered on the primary. The equatorial frame is the primary equator. Each Laplace pole is specified by source-specific right ascension and declination in the ICRF.
Small-body frames are preserved as EQ (equatorial, ICRF) and EC (Earth mean ecliptic). The catalogue equinox, usually J2000, is recorded if present.

orbitCoverage=elements requires a,e,i,node,argument of periapsis,mean anomaly,period,epoch and reference plane. partial records have one or more source values but cannot be used for an independently phased 3D orbit. No absent phase or inclination has been filled.

radiusKm uses JPL equivalent-volume mean radii for the planetary table or one half the published effective diameter for small-body satellites. Individual axis lengths, upper bounds and any estimates are not promoted to a radius. Unknown fields remain null.

Small-body records preserve JPL confirmed=Y/N. An unnamed record does not imply a formal provisional designation. Names and provisional designations are kept directly from sources, never synthesized from a host’s current permanent designation. systemIndex only enumerates records within the host and is not an IAU satellite number.

The small-body API catalogues the discovery/provisional year in prov_year. NASA Lucy gives the observed Selam discovery year as 2023; the JPL tabulated year is preserved as catalogYear. The NASA Hubble publication identifies Eurybates’s JPL S/2018 (3548) 1 as Queta.
Satellite explorer identifiers are local reference keys. For JPL planetary records, code is the NAIF satellite code. Small-body jplPrimaryId identifies the host, not its satellite.
